title: Pyramus and Thisbe
author: Ovid
source: Metamorphoses, Book IV (Translated by Sir Samuel Garth & John Dryden)
citation: Ovid. Metamorphoses, Book IV. Translated by Sir Samuel Garth and John Dryden, 1717.

sections.heading: The Whispering Wall and the Secret Vow

epigraph.quote: Cruel wall, why dost thou part two lovers who seek only to share a single embrace?

paragraphs: In ancient Babylon, Pyramus, the most handsome of youths, and Thisbe, the loveliest of maidens, lived in adjoining houses. As they grew from childhood into adolescence, friendship blossomed into passionate love. They longed to unite in holy matrimony, but their hostile fathers strictly forbade their union, building high brick walls between their properties.

Love, however, is ingenious and cannot be sealed away. In the shared party wall of their homes, a hairline chink had developed during its original construction. Through this tiny fissure, Pyramus and Thisbe whispered words of devotion morning and night. Desperate to escape parental tyranny, they agreed to steal away under cover of darkness the following night and meet beneath the spreading branches of a tall white mulberry tree beside King Ninus's tomb.

sections.heading: The Tragic Misunderstanding and the Mulberry Tree

epigraph.quote: The snowy white berries of the mulberry tree were dyed forever dark and crimson with the blood of two faithful hearts.

paragraphs: Veiled in secrecy, Thisbe reached the tomb first. As she waited in the shadows, a lioness fresh from slaughtering cattle approached the nearby spring to drink, her jaws dripping with blood. Terrified, Thisbe fled into a dark cave for refuge, accidentally dropping her silk veil in her haste. The lioness found the dropped garment and tore it with her bloody jaws before returning to the forest.

Arriving moments later, Pyramus discovered the lioness's tracks in the sand and saw Thisbe's blood-soaked, shredded veil. Believing his beloved dead and holding himself entirely responsible for her demise, Pyramus unsheathed his sword and plunged it into his breast. His warm blood spurted outward, soaking the roots of the mulberry tree and turning its hanging white berries deep purple.

When Thisbe cautiously emerged from the cave, she found Pyramus dying in the dust. Weeping inconsolably, she pressed his fading lips to hers, grasped his sword, and plunged it into her own heart so they might remain united in death. In pity, the gods ordained that the fruit of the mulberry tree would remain forever dark in remembrance of their tragic sacrifice.
